title: Catching Many Traitors in Threshold Traitor Tracing: Lower Bounds and Constructions
authors: Dan Boneh, Aditi Partap, and Mark Zhandry
abstract:
A $t$-out-of-$n$ threshold decryption scheme distributes decryption key shares among $n$ parties so that any $t$ of them can jointly decrypt a ciphertext, while fewer than $t$ learn nothing about the plaintext. Traditional threshold schemes provide no accountability: a coalition of $t$ or more parties can combine their key shares and construct a pirate decoder that decrypts arbitrary well-formed ciphertexts, without any risk of being traced. To address this, Boneh, Partap, and Rotem [CRYPTO '24] introduced the notion of threshold traitor tracing (TTT), where a tracing algorithm that is given black-box access to the pirate decoder can identify at least one of the colluding parties. Many subsequent threshold traitor tracing schemes similarly find only a single traitor, even though the decoder must have been constructed using at least $t$ keys. While some constructions can find multiple traitors, they do so at the cost of large ciphertexts or only achieving a weak form of correctness.

In this work, we make the following contributions:

- Lower bounds: We show that for all existing traitor tracing techniques, the ciphertext must be large to allow tracing close to $t$ traitors. In particular, to trace $t-O(1)$ traitors, the ciphertext size must be at least $\Omega(t)$. To trace $a \leq t- \omega(1)$ traitors, the ciphertext size must scale with $\Omega(\frac{a-1}{t-a+1})$. For schemes that rely on fingerprinting codes, we show an even stronger lower bound.

- Upper bounds: We present two generic compilers that construct traitor tracing for general access structures (beyond threshold) from two building blocks: attribute based encryption for general access structures and sufficiently-expressive policies and mixed functional-encryption. We also present two concrete instantiations. Under exponential security assumptions, we construct a pairings-based threshold traitor tracing scheme that can trace $t$ traitors with ciphertext size $O(t^2)$. We also construct an LWE-based traitor tracing scheme for a DNF access structure, that can trace an authorized subset of traitors with ciphertext size $O(\hat{t}^2)$, where $\hat{t}$ denotes the size of the largest unauthorized subset in the access structure.

-  A Candidate Theoretical Instantiation: We present a new tracing mechanism that can trace $t(1-1/\lambda^c)$ traitors with $\mathsf{poly}(\lambda)$ size ciphertext, public key, and secret keys. We prove security assuming ideal (black box) obfuscation.

Our work raises several open questions in the context of tracing multiple parties in a threshold traitor tracing scheme.

1   Introduction

Traitor tracing [CFN94] is an encryption system where the key generation algorithm outputs a
public key and n secret keys sk1 , . . . , skn , one key per user. Every secret key, on its own, can
decrypt a well-formed ciphertext. The central property is that if a coalition of parties J ⊆ [n] use
their secret keys {ski }i∈J to build a decryption algorithm D, then this D can be traced to at least
one of the parties in J . The tracing algorithm has black-box access to D and should output the
index of a party i ∈ J with overwhelming probability. Constructions try to optimize the public key,
secret key, and ciphertext sizes. A number of impressive works give constructions where all three
grow at most poly-logarithmically in the number of users n [GKW18, CVW+ 18, Zha25, BZ14].
Some constructions use fingerprinting codes [BS95, Tar03] to achieve constant size ciphertexts (i.e.,
independent of n), but then the secret key size is Ω(n) [BN08, BP08].
    Traitor tracing is intended to deter users from creating a decryption algorithm D that they
can sell to interested parties. If they do, the tracing algorithm applied to D will catch at least one
of them. Clearly the tracing algorithm cannot be required to catch more than one member of J .
Indeed, if only one secret key in J is sufficient to construct D, then the tracing algorithm can at
most trace D to that single key. Other members of J cannot be reliably blamed.

Threshold traitor tracing. With the growing use of threshold decryption, Boneh, Partap, and
Rotem [BPR24a] defined the notion of Threshold Traitor Tracing (TTT) — traitor tracing for
threshold decryption. Here again the key generation algorithm outputs a public key and n secret
keys. However, t secret keys are needed to decrypt a well-formed ciphertext, while t − 1 secret keys
cannot. If a coalition of t or more users get together to create a decryption algorithm D, then a
tracing algorithm can trace D to at least one member of the coalition that created D. This again
is meant to deter decryption parties from creating and selling a decryption algorithm to interested
parties. Boneh, Partap, and Rotem [BPR24a] gave several efficient constructions for TTT. Subse-
quent work strengthened the TTT security model to provide chosen ciphertext security [BBF+ 25],
public tracing [CPP25], silent setup [BHO25, CMMS25], and poly-log parameters [DDP+ 25].
    In all these works, however, the tracing algorithm is only required to trace D to a single member
of J . In the context of threshold traitor tracing, a decryption algorithm D must be constructed
from at least t secret keys. Therefore, it is reasonable to require the tracing algorithm to output
at least t traitors. This is a much harder problem than tracing to a single party. If it can be done,
it provides a stronger deterrence against selling a pirate decryption algorithm. Moreover, tracing t
traitors is what one would expect from threshold traitor tracing.
    In this paper, we focus on the problem of tracing t traitors, which we call multi-tracing. Some
constructions already support multi-tracing, but with some limitations. The works of [BPR24a]
and [BHO25] point out that the trivial threshold traitor tracing scheme, with O(n) size ciphertexts,
supports tracing D to at least t members of J . Bormet, Faust, and Othman [BFO26] show how to
trace D to multiple traitors, with sub-linear ciphertext size, but their construction only achieves
weak correctness: only a random set of t parties can decrypt, not every set of t parties. The question
is whether multi-tracing can be done with short ciphertexts and complete correctness.

1.1   Our Results: Lower Bounds
We begin with two lower bounds on the ciphertext size for threshold traitor tracing schemes that
trace D to multiple users. These lower bounds correspond to two different tracing techniques:
subset-based tracing and tracing based on fingerprinting codes.

Subset-based Tracing We first consider a restricted but very general class of threshold traitor
tracing algorithms that we call “subset-based.” In such a scheme, every ciphertext c is associated
with a certain subset of parties Sx ⊆ [n]. A set of t parties J ⊆ [n] can decrypt c if and only
if J ⊆ Sx . Normally, one encrypts a message µ with respect to the entire set of parties [n], so
that every subset of t parties can decrypt. However, during tracing, the tracing algorithm will
query the decryption algorithm D with ciphertexts targeting different subsets Sx , and then observe
whether D successfully decrypts or not. This approach captures all existing threshold traitor tracing
schemes [BPR24a, DDP+ 25, CMMS25, BHO25, BBF+ 25, BFO26], as well as existing non-threshold
traitor tracing schemes (e.g., [BN08, BSW06, GLW23, Zha21, GKW18, CVW+ 18, Zha25, BZ14])
that do not make any stipulations about the decoder program.

Theorem 1 (Informal). For a threshold traitor tracing scheme with subset-based tracing for n
parties and threshold t,
 – If the scheme can trace t − O(1) traitors, then the ciphertext size must grow with t log(λ).
 – If the scheme can trace a ≤ t − ω(1) traitors, for large n, the ciphertext size must scale with
     a−1
   t−a+1 ω(log λ).
 – If the scheme is universal, meaning the tracing algorithm is independent of the decoder box (and
   in particular, traces boxes running in super-polynomial time), then, the ciphertext size must
   scale with (a − 1) log2 (n/t).

Fingerprinting Code-based Tracing Fingerprinting codes, originally introduced in [BS95], have
been used to build traitor tracing [BN08, BP08, Zha20] and more recently, threshold traitor trac-
ing [BPR24a, BBF+ 25], albeit for catching one traitor. We first introduce the notion of multi-
fingerprinting codes, which is a generalization of fingerprinting codes that allows tracing multiple
traitors. (Threshold) traitor tracing based on such codes is a special case of subset-based traitor
tracing, and is therefore subject to the lower-bound in Theorem 1. However, we are able to show
an even stronger lower-bound for such schemes:

Theorem 2 (Informal). For a threshold traitor tracing scheme based on multi-fingerprinting
codes, that can trace a ≤ t traitors, the ciphertext size must scale with Ω(t · (n/t)a/t ). In particular,
for a = t, the ciphertext size must be Ω(n).

   While this result applies only to fingerprinting codes-based schemes, it gives stronger lower
bounds than Theorem 1.

1.2   Our Results: Upper Bounds
Next, we present two generic compilers to construct traitor tracing for general access structures,
that can trace to an authorized subset of parties. In particular, for the threshold access structure,
we are guaranteed to find t traitors. We then present two concrete instantiations based on our
compilers. Lastly, we give a candidate theoretical instantiation based on a new tracing mechanism.
Our Compilers. Our compilers rely on two building blocks: (i) Attribute-based Encryption for
general access structures and sufficiently-expressive key policies: this is a generalization of Attribute-
based Encryption wherein each party is issued a key associated with a policy and an index, while
ciphertexts are labeled with attributes. Decryption succeeds only if a quorum of parties autho-
rized with respect to the access structure comes together, all holding keys whose policies accept
the ciphertext’s attribute. (ii) Mixed Functional Encryption: this is a special type of functional
encryption scheme introduced by [GKW18], wherein the encryption algorithm works with either a
public key or master secret key. Ciphertexts encrypted using the public key can only encrypt one
type of functionality. On the other hand the secret key encryption can be used to encode many
different types of functions, but is only secure as long as the attacker sees a bounded number of
such ciphertexts.

Theorem 3 (Informal). Assume there exists
 – Mixed Functional Encryption for a special comparison function class, that achieves adaptive
   security for poly(λ) number of secret-key encryption queries and,

                                                    3
 – adaptively secure attribute-based encryption for general access structures, that can support the
   policy class of the MFE decryption circuit.
Then, there exists a traitor tracing scheme for general access structures, which allows tracing to
a set of authorized traitors. The ciphertext size scales polynomially with the size of the largest
unauthorized subset in the access structure.

    Our next compiler only requires adaptive security for the mixed functional encryption scheme
wherein the adversary is allowed to make only one secret key encryption query (as opposed to
poly(λ) in the previous compiler):

Theorem 4 (Informal). Assume there exists
 – Mixed Functional Encryption for a special comparison function class, that achieves adaptive
   security for 1-secret key encryption query and,
 – adaptively secure attribute-based encryption for general access structures, that can support the
   policy class of the MFE decryption circuit.
Then, there exists a traitor tracing scheme for general access structures, which allows tracing to
a set of authorized traitors. The ciphertext size scales polynomially with the size of the largest
unauthorized subset in the access structure.

Concrete Instantiations. Since all existing constructions of mixed functional encryption and
attribute based encryption for general access structures only achieve selective security, we use
complexity leveraging to instantiate our compilers. We get the following two results:

Theorem 5. Under exponential security assumptions, there exists a pairings-based threshold traitor
tracing scheme that can trace t traitors with ciphertext size O(t2 ).

Theorem 6. Under exponential security assumptions, there exists a lattice-based traitor tracing
scheme for DNF access structures that can trace an authorized subset of traitors with ciphertext
size O(t2 ), where t denotes the size of the largest unauthorized subset in the access structure.

Candidate theoretical instantiation. The above positive results for threshold tracing all have
ciphertexts growing with t; this is inherent by Theorem 1 for two reasons: they all trace t users,
and they all employ universal tracing where the tracing algorithm is independent of the box itself,
and in particular independent of the box’s run-time.
   Our final positive result gives a candidate tracing mechanism based on obfuscation, which traces
a < t users by utilizing a non-universal tracing algorithm, and essentially matches Theorem 1:

Theorem 7 (Informal). For any constant c > 0, assuming one-way functions and ideal (black
box) obfuscation, there exists a threshold traitor tracing scheme whose ciphertext, public key, and
secret key sizes are all poly(λ), independent of n and t, which traces a = (1 − λ−c )t users.

1.3   Additional Related Work

Traceability in Other Primitives. [GSS21] introduced the notion of traceability in secret
sharing, wherein a less-than-threshold number of share holders may sell their shares to an adversary.
There has been a lot of work on building traceable secret sharing schemes with different efficiency

                                                 4
and security tradeoffs [BPR24b, GJP25, Hof24, FG25, FG26]. [BPR25] study traceability in the
context of threshold verifiable random functions, wherein a coalition of less-than-threshold parties
may sell their VRF evaluation key shares. [DPP20] generalize the notion of traitor tracing to
functional encryption.

2     Technical Overview

In this section, we present an overview of our contributions. We start with discussing the models
for the lower bounds in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, before presenting our compilers in Section 2.3 and
concrete instantiations in Section 2.4 and 2.5. We discuss open problems in Section 2.6.

2.1    Lower Bound on Subset-based Tracing

For our first lower bound, we consider a special case of threshold traitor tracing, which we call
subset-based tracing. As we will see later in this section, this captures all existing (threshold) traitor
tracing mechanisms that only use the decoder box D as a black-box, which in turn constitute almost
all existing traitor tracing methods.
The  model. In a subset-based threshold traitor tracing scheme, there is a collection of subsets
S = Sx ⊆ [n] x∈I where [n] ∈ S. For any subset Sx ∈ S, one can create a ciphertext c so that
a set of parties J ⊂ [n] can decrypt c if and only if J ⊆ Sx and |J | ≥ t. In other words, for
every ciphertext, there is a subset of users Sx that are “authorized” to decrypt that ciphertext.
Under normal operations, one encrypts the message µ using the set [n] so that every quorum of t
parties can decrypt. However, during tracing, the tracing algorithm will query the decoder D with
ciphertexts targeting specific subsets Sx ∈ S.
Intuition for tracing in the subset-based model. In a subset-based traitor tracing scheme,
the tracing algorithm tries D on various ciphertexts which “turn off” certain users (namely, those
excluded from Sx ), and sees if D still manages to decrypt. For example, maybe t = 3 and Sx =
{1, 4, 5, 7}. Then any three users in Sx , such as {1, 5, 7}, will be able to decrypt the ciphertext,
while three users not fully contained in Sx , such as {1, 4, 10}, will not be able to decrypt. Thus,
whether or not the decoder is able to decrypt such ciphertexts can reveal information about the
set of keys in the decoder’s possession.
Applicability to existing tracing schemes. Theorem 1 shows a lower bound on the ciphertext
size for subset-based threshold traitor tracing schemes that allow tracing multiple traitors. We now
discuss how this lower bound applies to all existing tracing techniques:
 – Private Linear Broadcast Encryption (PLBE): PLBE was first introduced by [BSW06] in the
   context of traitor tracing. But recently, many threshold traitor tracing schemes [BPR24a,
   DDP+ 25, CMMS25, BHO25] have been constructed based on PLBE techniques. At a high
   level, in (threshold) traitor tracing based on PLBE, the tracer has the ability (using its secret
   key) to create ciphertexts associated with intervals, i.e. Sx = {i ∈ [n] : i ≤ y} for various values
   of y ∈ {0, . . . , n}. The tracer then runs the decoder box on such ciphertexts.
 – Revocable PLBE: [Zha20, GLW23] use a revocable version of PLBE to achieve non-threshold
   traitor tracing, and this was adapted to the threshold case in [BPR24a]. While the set system
   {Sx } that can be associated with a ciphertext is more complex than the set of intervals as in
   standard PLBE, the schemes are an instance of the subset-based tracing paradigm.

                                                    5
 – Fingerprinting codes: To understand (threshold) traitor tracing constructions based on finger-
   printing codes, let us consider the trivial scheme for t = 1 based on binary fingerprinting codes.
   Herein, we sample two public keys for an encryption scheme for each position of the codeword,
   corresponding to bits 0 and 1. Then, party i is assigned a subset Ui of the secret keys, based on
   its codeword: for every position j, it gets the key corresponding to the jth bit of its codeword.
   A ciphertext encrypts a message to a random position j of the codeword, which can be inter-
   preted as an encryption to a subset Cj of the keys, corresponding to both keys for this position.
   Observe that for each user, |Ui ∩ Cj | = 1.
   The tracer additionally has the ability to encrypt messages with respect to either the bit 0
   or 1 for a position j. Only parties whose jth bit of the codeword matches the bit that the
   tracer encrypted towards, can decrypt this ciphertext. Such a ciphertext can also be interpret
   as encrypting to a subset Tj of the keys corresponding to position j. Then, we can define Sx
   for such a ciphertext as the set of parties i that satisfy Ui ∩ Tj ̸= ∅, since only these parties can
   decrypt such a ciphertext. While we discussed the case of t = 1, the above intuition also applies
   to threshold traitor tracing based on fingerprinting codes as constructed in [BPR24a]. Hence,
   the fingerprinting-code based tracing is also an instance of the subset-based tracing paradigm.
 – Non-black-box Tracing: All existing threshold traitor tracing schemes, including the ones dis-
   cussed above, only allow the tracer to have black-box access to the decoder. However, in the
   case of non-threshold traitor tracing, some past works have considered a non-black-box variant
   wherein the tracing algorithm has access to the the actual code of the decoder. Some early
   traitor tracing works (e.g. see [KD98, BF99, NP01, TS06, JKL09, ADVW13] and the references
   therein) worked in this model, but they all made strong assumptions on the decoder – essen-
   tially that the decoder took the form of a decryption key. The only prior work which makes
   non-black-box use of truly arbitrary decoder programs is that of [Zha21]. [Zha21] technically
   does not fall under the category of subset-based traitor tracing, as it actually utilizes the code
   of the decoder as opposed to directly making queries. However, the tracing algorithm actually is
   querying the decoder on ciphertexts, just implicitly by performing the query homomorphically.
   The ciphertexts that are homomorphically queried follow the format of a subset-based traitor
   tracing scheme. Thus, while [Zha21] does not technically fit the form of a subset-based scheme,
   it effectively is. In particular, the limits we prove on subset-based schemes will apply to any
   protocols based on ideas in [Zha21].
Thus, we see that all existing tracing mechanisms that do not make any stipulations about the
decoder program can be considered subset-based schemes. This includes both the recent threshold
schemes, as well as the vast body of work on non-threshold schemes. Hence, our lower bound in
Theorem 1 applies quite generally to all such techniques. The precise statement of the lower bound
and its proof can be found in Section 4.

2.2   Lower Bound on Fingerprinting-based Tracing
In this section, we focus on tracing based on fingerprinting codes. We start with describing what
fingerprinting codes are and how they are useful for tracing.
Background on Traitor Tracing from Fingerprinting codes. A fingerprinting code for al-
phabet Σ is a set of words where Γ = (w1 , . . . , wn ) wherein each word is of length ℓ, i.e. wi ∈ Σ ℓ .
Let us consider Σ = {0, 1} for now. What makes fingerprinting codes special is that they come
equipped with a tracing algorithm Trace that has the following functionality. Say that an adversary

                                                   6
is in possession of a subset of words W ⊆ Γ , and it comes up with a word w∗ that is constructed
by mixing and matching the bits of the words in W . That is, if for some index i ∈ [ℓ], the ith bit
of all words in W is 0, then the ith bit of w∗ must be 0 as well (and similarly if the ith bit of all
words is 1). We call such a word feasible for W . The guarantee of fingerprinting codes is that the
Trace algorithm can trace such a word w∗ back to at least one of the words in W .
    Equipped with such a code, Boneh and Naor showed how to construct a (non-threshold) traitor
tracing scheme from any public key encryption scheme E. The idea is to generate 2ℓ independent
key pairs for E – let us index them using (j, b) for j ∈ [ℓ], b ∈ {0, 1}. The overall public key contains
all 2ℓ public keys, and the secret key for party i contains one key for each j ∈ [ℓ], depending on the
jth position of the word wi . In particular, party i receives {skj,wi [j] }j∈[ℓ] . To encrypt a message, one
chooses a random position j ←$ [ℓ], and encrypts the message under both keys for this position, to
get (c0 , c1 ).
    Tracing relies on the observation that, thanks to the semantic security of E, a coalition of
parties holding only skj,0 cannot distinguish between an honestly generated ciphertext (c0 , c1 ) and
a ciphertext (c0 , c′1 ) where c′1 is an encryption to some random message. The same goes for a coalition
holding only skj,1 . This observation can be used to extract a word w∗ from a pirate decoder D with
the property that w∗ is indeed feasible for the set of words associated with the corrupted coalition.
Hence, we can rely on the tracing algorithm of the fingerprinting code to trace D back to one of
the corrupted parties. While the above exposition only applies for the case t = 1, [BPR24a] show
how to extend this idea to get threshold traitor tracing for arbitrary t using fingerprinting codes.
Generally speaking, the ciphertext size scales with the alphabet size |Σ|, and the secret key size
scales with the length of the code ℓ.

The model for lower bound: multi-Fingerprinting Codes. The above idea is fundamentally
limited to trace only one party, since the Trace algorithm of the code only guarantees to trace one
party given a feasible word. If we wish to recover more than one traitors, we need a fingerprinting
code capable of identifying multiple users. We first observe that given a single feasible word, it is
impossible to trace multiple users, since the word w∗ might equal one of the words in W , in which
case we can only trace to the party corresponding to that word. Hence, we consider a scenario
wherein the cryptography allows us to extract more information from the decoder box, beyond a
single feasible word w∗ . In particular, we imagine that we extract a subset Σj ⊆ Σ of symbols for
each position j ∈ [ℓ] (as opposed to just a single symbol i.e. one bit for each position), with the
guarantee that the box must possess at least t codewords whose symbols at that position belong
in the subset Σj . For instance, if we extract a ‘1’ at a position j ∈ [ℓ], then the box must have t
parties whose codeword has a ‘1’ at this position. We refer to the subset of symbols per position as
a multi-word, and we say that it is feasible for a set of words W if the above guarantee holds with
respect to W .
    We define a generalization of fingerprinting codes, that we call multi-fingerprinting codes,
wherein the tracing algorithm takes as input a multi-word that is feasible for a set of words W , and
traces it to a subset of W of size t. Our lower bound then proves that for a multi-fingerprinting code,
we must either have a large alphabet, or an exponentially-long code. Since an exponentially-long
code would lead to exponential-size secret keys, this means that we must have a large alphabet,
hence giving a lower bound on the ciphertext size for schemes based on multi-fingerprinting codes.
We refer the reader to Section 5 for more details.

2.3   Upper Bound: Tracing many users by generalizing PLBE
In this section, we describe our generic compilers for building traitor tracing for general access struc-
tures. We start with presenting the constructions for threshold, before discussing how to generalize
the idea to general access structures. We present our concrete instantiations in Section 2.4.
Starting Point: TTT from TPLBE to trace one party. Our starting point is a generic compiler
to build threshold traitor tracing that can trace one party, from a primitive called threshold Private
Linear Broadcast Encryption (PLBE), given in [DDP+ 25]. A threshold PLBE system for n parties
has a public key pk, master secret key msk, and secret keys of all parties sk1 , sk2 , . . . , skn . Messages
in PLBE can be either encrypted in a public-key mode or a secret-key mode. The public-key mode
encryption (which we also refer to as the normal encryption) requires only the public-key pk and
the underlying message, and any t parties can decrypt such public-key mode ciphertexts using their
secret keys {skj }. To encrypt in the secret-key mode, the secret-key encryption algorithm, EncSK,
takes as input msk, a message and an index i, and outputs a ciphertext that can only be decrypted
by t users with indices greater than i. We call such a ciphertext a secret-key encryption with respect
to the set {i + 1, . . . , n}. In other words, this ciphertext disables parties ≤ i.
    Threshold PLBE must satisfy four security properties. The first is the standard notion of seman-
tic security, which says that an adversary that corrupts up to t − 1 parties, must not learn anything
about the encrypted message. The second is index-hiding, which requires that an adversary with
keys of all parties except i, cannot distinguish between secret-key encryptions to index i − 1 and i.
The third is message-hiding, which requires that secret-key encryptions of two different messages
m0 , m1 to index n must be indistinguishable, even if the adversary has all n keys. Lastly, indistin-
guishability requires that a normal encryption of message m created using pk is indistinguishable
from a EncSK encryption of m to the index 0, even if the adversary has all n keys.
      [DDP+ 25] show how one can build Threshold Traitor Tracing that allows tracing one corrupt
party from Threshold PLBE. For setup, we run the setup algorithm of threshold PLBE, and give
secret key ski to party i. The master secret key becomes the tracing key. Any message can be
encrypted via the public-key mode of threshold PLBE; and this can be decrypted by any t parties.
To trace a decoder box D, the tracing algorithm measures (with several samples) the probability
that D correctly decrypts a ciphertext encrypted in the secret-key mode to index i for all i ∈ [0, n].
In other words, the tracer tries to disable parties one by one and observes the decoder’s behavior.
If the box D decrypts public-key ciphertexts with probability ϵ, then it must decrypt ciphertexts
encrypted to index 0 with roughly the same probability, by indistinguishability. Moreover, D cannot
decrypt encryptions to index n, by message-hiding. Hence, there must exist some index i∗ ∈ [n]
where D’s success probability drops significantly between encryptions to index i∗ − 1 and i∗ . By
index-hiding, this gap implies D must contain ski∗ ; hence, the tracer simply outputs i∗ as a traitor.
Tracing Multiple Parties. Let us now see how we can extend the above framework to trace t
parties. Let i∗ denote the traitor found via the procedure above. The key observation is that, if we
repeat the same procedure as above, i.e. disabling parties one by one, but without ever disabling
the party i∗ that we already found, then we can catch another traitor! In more detail, say that
the tracer has the ability to prepare secret-key encryptions with respect to sets {1, . . . , n} ∪ {i∗ },
{2, . . . , n}∪{i∗ }, and so on till ∅∪{i∗ } (we will discuss how to extend threshold PLBE to enable this

A new primitive: Threshold Private Set Broadcast Encryption (TPSBE). To formalize
the above intuition, we introduce a new primitive that we call Threshold Private Set Broadcast
Encryption. This is a generalization of TPLBE, wherein we can encrypt messages in the secret-key
mode to an index i and a set T , to produce a ciphertext that can only be decrypted by t users with
indices in {i + 1, . . . , n} ∪ T . In other words, t parties all of which are either > i or in the set T
can decrypt such a ciphertext.

is semantic security, which is defined exactly as for TPLBE. Next, we have set-hiding, which is a
generalization of index-hiding. Informally, it requires that an adversary cannot distinguish between
encryptions to index-set pairs (i0 , T0 ) and (i1 , T1 ), even if it is given the secret keys of all parties
that are either enabled with respect to both encryptions or disabled for both. More formally, the
adversary is allowed to get secret keys of all parties in the following set:

even if the adversary has all n keys. This captures the following intuition: For a ciphertext encrypted
to (n, T ), only the parties in T are enabled with respect to this ciphertext. But since T has less
than t parties, this ciphertext cannot be decrypted.

created using pk is indistinguishable from a secret-key encryption with respect to index-set pair

this property wherein we could consider encryptions using pk vs encryptions to (0, T ) for arbitrary
sets T , the weaker notion we consider above turns out to be sufficient for catching t parties in
threshold traitor tracing.

2.5     A Candidate for tracing many users with optimal parameters

Here, we very briefly explain how we achieve Theorem 7. The tracing algorithms above followed a
natural blueprint of trying to turn off all users but the accused users. It is not hard to see that, since
the set of accused users can be truly arbitrary, and the ciphertext must (information-theoretically)
encode the set of accused/turned-on users, that ciphertexts must grow with the number of accused
users. However, for a number of accused users a only somewhat smaller than t, namely a = (1−λ−c )t,
the lower bound in Theorem 1 becomes vacuous.
    Our idea to trace a users is, very roughly, to keep the accused users turned on, but only turn
off a small but random subset of the other users. Of course, even describing a truly random small
set of users to turn off will require large ciphertexts. But here, since the set is random, we can
pseudorandomly sample which users to turn off. In fact, we will pseudorandomly sample the turned
off users from among all possible users, including the users already accused, and then simply sample
again in the event that any of the accused users fail to be turned on. This allows us to describe
the set of turned on/off users succinctly using a pseudorandom function. The key to efficiency is
ensuring that the number trials to produce a good sample remains polynomial. It turns out that
the number of samples remains efficient for a = (1 − λ−c )t for a constant c, and the lower-bound
in Theorem 1 shows that we cannot do any better.
    To actually implement this idea, we employ candidate cryptographic obfuscation. To justify
security, we model the obfuscated program as an ideal black-box, similar to the notion of virtual-
black box (VBB) obfuscation. While ideal/VBB obfuscation are known to be impossible for general
programs [BGI+ 01], the counterexamples are contrived and involve self-referential programs. Our
programs do not have this flavor, and so it is plausible that our scheme is secure despite the
impossibilities. There are notable barriers to proving security under a standard obfuscation notion
such as indistinguishability obfuscation (iO). We give our full protocol and discuss these barriers
in Section 10.

7     Constructing PSBE for General Access Structures

In this section, we present a generic compiler to construct PSBE for general access structures from
(i) a mixed FE scheme and (ii) an attribute-based encryption for the same access structure. We
start with defining the two building blocks in Sections 7.1 and 7.2, before presenting the compilers

7.1    Attribute-based Encryption for General Access Structures

A (key-policy) Attribute-based Encryption for general access structures (ABEG) scheme for a
family of predicate classes P = {Pλ } and a family of access structures C = {Cλ }λ is a tuple of PPT
algorithms ABEG = (Setup, KeyGen, Enc, Dec, Combine):

 – Setup(1λ , C, 1z ) → (pk, msk) is the probabilistic setup algorithm that takes as inputs the secu-
   rity parameter λ ∈ N, the access structure in the form of a circuit C : {0, 1}n → {0, 1} such that
   C ∈ Cλ , the attribute length parameter z ∈ N, and outputs the public key pk and the master
   secret key msk.
 – KeyGen(msk, i, P ) → skiP is the probabilistic key generation algorithm that takes as inputs
   an index i, the master secret key msk, a predicate P ∈ Pλ representing a policy, and outputs a
   secret key skiP for index i with respect to this policy. For any attribute x, we use P (x) = 1 to
   denote that x satisfies this predicate.
 – Enc(pk, µ, x) → ctx is the probabilistic encryption algorithm that takes as inputs the pub-
   lic key pk, the plain text message µ, an attribute x and outputs a ciphertext ctx . We may
   use Enc(pk, µ, x; r) to denote the deterministic version of this algorithm, which takes as input
   randomness r sampled from a randomness space R.
 – Dec(skiP , ctx ) → di is the probabilistic decryption algorithm that takes as input a secret key
   skiP for some index i and policy P , a ciphertext ctx generated with respect to attribute x and
   outputs the partial decryption di of ctx under skiP .
 – Combine(pk, ctx , {dj }j∈S ) → µ is the deterministic combiner algorithm that takes as inputs a
   set of decryption shares {dj }j∈S for a set S ⊆ [n] of size t and outputs a message µ.

10.1   Challenges for Provable Security
Here, we discuss what seem to be challenges in turning our candidate into a provably-secure con-
struction. We first start with a seemingly minor obstacle, which we believe is not the main bottle-
neck.

The Turing Machine Bottleneck. First, we used obfuscation for Turing machines, but direct obfus-
cation constructions are for circuits. In the ideal/virtual black box setting where the obfuscated
program is heuristically treated as an oracle, Turing machine obfuscation follows readily from cir-
cuit obfuscation. However, for the standard notion of indistinguishability obfuscation (iO), existing
constructions of Turing machine obfuscation (e.g. [AJS17]) restrict the input to a bounded size L,
and the obfuscated program grows polynomially in L. In our case, the input to P is a list of t
decryption values, and so existing solutions would result in a program growing with t.
    We believe this limitation is not fundamental, though we omitted attempts to resolve it due
to the more fundamental difficulties below making it unclear what a provable construction would
look like. First, one can move the obfuscated program from ciphertext into the public key; now
the ciphertext encrypts the hard-coded k1 , · · · , kλc as well as the message µ using a CCA secure
encryption scheme. The obfuscated program in the public key contains the decryption key, decrypts
the ciphertext, and outputs µ only if the various checks pass. This allows us to achieve short
ciphertexts, but still results in large public keys if using circuit obfuscation. To further compress
the public key, we expect various techniques from the obfuscation literature to be useful. For
example, the program P could take as input a succinct commitment to the set J , together with
a single decryption value di . It will output a decryption share associated with the set J , and the
share will be valid if and only if i is “turned on.” Then outside of the obfuscated program, the
decryption shares will be used to reconstruct the message the message µ, but reconstruction will
only succeed if all the decryption shares are valid and all are associated with the same J .

The Decoder Run-time Barrier. Now we turn to the more significant barrier. Namely, observe
that Lemma 20 depends on the number of queries made by the decoder. In particular, Lemma 20
combined with Lemma 21 are invoked in a regime of parameters where the success probability is non-
negligible but depends polynomially on the run-time of the decoder. Such statements are difficult to
make with standard techniques in the literature. For example, an actual decoder may not work by
explicitly querying the obfuscated code on various inputs, but may be able to extract information
from a super-polynomial number of inputs in polynomial time. This would not contradict any
statement that could be proved using iO together with standard cryptographic tools. But if the
decoder could extract such information, it would invalidate our tracing guarantee.
    A promising direction would be to use an exponentially-hard primitive, and scale the security
parameter down to a logarithmic value depending on the decoder run-time. Exponential hardness
used in this way allows for making the kind of fine-grained statements we would need for trac-
ing; for an example see [Zha16]. Even using existing techniques involving exponential hardness,
however, it seems non-trivial to prove our candidate secure, due to the structure of our tracing
mechanism. Roughly, it seems that we would need an exponentially-secure obfuscation for the sub-
set containment functionality, which can be obtained by techniques in [BKM+ 18, BLMZ19, GZ19].
Importantly, we need the obfuscation to be “optimally secure” in the sense that it is impossible
to speed up finding an accepting input much faster than generic attacks. Unfortunately, the only
constructions we have are proven in generic models, and also result in very big objects, growing
with the universe size, which corresponds to the number of users.
